history_of_present_illness: Filarial infections can range from asymptomatic carriage of numerous adult filariae and myriads of embryos to severe disease. Filaria bancrofti infection can manifest with elephantiasis, varicose groin glands, chyluria, irregular febrile conditions (elephantoid fever), lymph scrotum, filarial abscesses, and filarial orchitis and hydrocele. Recurring attacks of lymphangitis are common. Loa loa infection is characterized by the wandering of adult worms in subcutaneous tissues, particularly around the eyes, causing disagreeable sensations and an oedematous track. Clinical features include Calabar swellings (transient, painless, hen's egg sized, itchy, non-pitting), irregular febrile conditions, and transient painless swellings about joints associated with stiffness. Onchocerca volvulus typically causes subcutaneous tumors, most often found in the axilla, thorax, trochanters, or ilium. These masses usually cause little discomfort and do not tend to ulcerate, but may lead to keratitis in American infections. Acanthocheilonema perstans is generally considered non-pathogenic, though it may cause an irregular fever. Dracunculus medinensis (Guinea worm) infection causes a blister-like lesion, typically on the lower extremity, as the female worm presses against the skin. This lesion bursts, extruding embryos. Symptoms include discomfort from the blister, a feeling of heaviness in the affected extremity, and at times, pain and fever. If the worm fails to exit or dies, it may calcify or lead to abscess formation.
exposure_and_epidemiology: Filarial worms are thread-like nematodes. Their geographical distribution and transmission methods vary by species: Filaria bancrofti is found in almost all tropical and subtropical countries, including the West Indies, Southern U.S., Central and South America, Arabia, India, China, West Africa, Australia (Queensland), and Pacific islands (Samoa, Fiji, Philippines). It is transmitted by mosquitoes, primarily Culex fatigans and Stegomyia pseudoscutellaris, and also M. ludlowi and M. rossii. Larvae escape from the mosquito's proboscis and enter human skin. Loa loa is currently confined to the West Coast of Africa (Cameroons, Old Calabar). It is transmitted by species of biting flies (Chrysops). Cases were historically reported in the West Indies from infected slaves. Acanthocheilonema perstans has been found in natives of the Congo and British Guiana. Its transmitting agent is not surely known, but mosquitoes and ticks have been suggested. Onchocerca volvulus is found principally on the West Coast of Africa and has been reported from Guatemala. Its method of transmission is unknown. Dracunculus medinensis (Guinea worm) is endemic in India, Arabia, the West Coast of Africa, and Brazil. Humans contract the infection by drinking water containing Cyclops (minute crustaceans) that have swallowed the embryos. Filaria demarquayi (also known as F. ozzardi) is an unimportant filarial worm found only in the West Indies and British Guiana.
vitals: Fever is a common manifestation in several filarial infections. Filaria bancrofti can cause 'elephantoid fever,' characterized by a high fever of sudden onset with rigors. Loa loa infection may present with irregular febrile conditions. An irregular fever has been suggested as a possible symptom of Acanthocheilonema perstans. Dracunculus medinensis can also cause fever at times.
physical_exam: Physical findings depend on the specific filarial species: Filaria bancrofti manifests as: - Elephantiasis: hypertrophy of the skin and subcutaneous tissues, rough skin, scanty hair, lymphoedema, and a great increase in connective tissue, most commonly affecting lower extremities (90%), but also upper extremities, scrotum, vulva, breasts, penis, scalp, neck, or trunk. Incision into affected tissue causes outpouring of lymph. - Lymph Scrotum: tense and reddened scrotal tissues, often showing numerous lymphatic varices that exude lymph (which may contain embryos) when pricked. Recurring attacks lead to hypertrophy and potential elephantiasis of the scrotum. Erysipelatous manifestations are not uncommon. - Varicose Groin Glands: slow-onset, insidious swellings involving inguinal or femoral gland groups (unilaterally or bilaterally), and sometimes epitrochlear glands. The skin over these enlarged, doughy glands is freely movable, but the glands are bound to deeper tissues. May be associated with pain and redness. Puncture yields lymph, possibly with embryos. - Filarial Abscesses: deep-seated, found in extremities, pelvis of the kidney, epididymis, retroperitoneal tissues, inguinal glands, ilio-psoas muscles, and lymphatic vessels. - Chyluria: milky urine, often with a pinkish tinge due to blood. Urine coagulates rapidly, forming an upper fatty layer, a pinkish sediment (containing lymphocytes and sometimes embryos), and a clot. - Filarial Orchitis and Hydrocele: resembles epididymitis, with hydrocele development; fluid may be lymphous or chylous and may contain embryos. Hydroceles do not become very large but may require tapping. Other lymphatic varices like chylous ascites or chylous diarrhoea can occur. Loa loa infection is characterized by: - Calabar Swellings: usually painless, sudden, transient, non-pitting oedematous swellings, about the size of a hen's egg, lasting ~3 days, causing marked tension and itching. Occur on thin-layered connective tissue areas like forearms, face, ankles, and hands. - Visible adult worms migrating in subcutaneous tissues, especially around the eyes and under the conjunctivae, often leaving an oedematous track. Onchocerca volvulus presents as: - Subcutaneous Tumors: firm, cyst-like masses, typically found in the axilla, sides of the thorax, over trochanters, or along the crests of the ilium. In American infections, tumors are more common near the eye. The skin is freely movable over them. Dracunculus medinensis infection typically shows: - A blister-like lesion, usually on the lower extremity, caused by the female worm pressing against the skin. This lesion subsequently ruptures, forming a small surface erosion from which the worm's uterus may protrude, extruding embryos upon contact with water. - X-ray imaging may reveal a convoluted cord-like structure with frequent breaks if the worm dies or calcifies.
labs_and_diagnostics: **Microscopic Examination for Microfilariae (Embryos)**: - **Blood Examination**: A fresh blood preparation from a finger prick or earlobe (with a vaseline ring and cover-glass) allows observation of living embryos for over a day. Smear preparations (Ehrlich, Daniels thick smear) can be made, dehaemoglobinized with water, and stained with dilute haematoxylin, Leishman’s, Wright’s, Giemsa’s, or haematoxylin (recommended for color retention). Ruge’s thick film method for malarial parasites also works. - **Morphological Identification**: - *Filaria bancrofti* embryos: Sheathed, 300 x 7.5 microns. Distance from head to V spot 90 microns; to break in cells (nerve ring) 50 microns. Tail is rather straight; terminal cells do not fill the tail end. Cell nuclei extend to 95% of total length. Anal pore at 82% of length. - *Loa loa* embryos: Sheathed, 240 x 7 microns. Distance from head to V spot 65 microns; to break in cells (nerve ring) 40 microns. Cork-screw tail completely filled with terminal cells. Curves show irregularities. - *Acanthocheilonema perstans* embryos: Without sheaths, 200 x 5 microns. Posterior two-thirds tapers to a blunt ending. Distance from head to V spot 49 microns; to break in cells 34 microns. - *Onchocerca volvulus* embryos: Without sheaths, 250 x 7.5 microns. Found in cyst-like spaces of tumors, rarely in peripheral circulation. Dubois reported them in juice from punctured groin glands. - *Dracunculus medinensis* embryos: Without sheaths, 600 x 20 microns. Long slender tail. Cuticle striated. Extruded from skin lesions. - **Periodicity**: *F. bancrofti* embryos typically show nocturnal periodicity in peripheral circulation (absent in Pacific Islands and Philippines). *L. loa* embryos show diurnal periodicity. *A. perstans* embryos persist in circulation both day and night. - **Fluid Examination**: Embryos may be found in lymph from varicose groin glands, exudate from chylous hydrocele, or urinary sediment from chyluria. - **Adult Worm Identification**: - *Filaria bancrofti* adults: Male 40 x 0.1 mm, female 90 x 0.28 mm. Smooth cuticle, bulbous anterior extremity. Occupy lymphatic glands and vessels. Can be found alive or calcified in lymphatic glands or filarial abscesses. - *Loa loa* adults: Male 27 x 0.3 mm, female 55 x 0.4 mm. Tuberculated cuticle, anterior extremity like truncated cone. Wander in subcutaneous tissues. Cuticular protuberances (bosses) 12-15 microns in height. - *Acanthocheilonema perstans* adults: Male 40 x 0.07 mm, female 75 x 0.1 mm. Smooth cuticle. Tip of tail shows 2 triangular processes. Found about the root of the mesentery, retroperitoneal connective tissue or fat. - *Onchocerca volvulus* adults: Male 30 x 0.14 mm, female possibly 75 x 0.36 mm. Cuticle striated. Found coiled in cyst-like tumors under the skin. - *Dracunculus medinensis* adults: Male ~22 mm. Female 80-90 cm long by 1.6 mm wide (up to 36 inches long, 1/15 inch diameter). Smooth white body, anchoring hook at tail end. Female lives in subcutaneous tissue. Body almost entirely uterus. **General Findings**: Blood examination usually shows eosinophilia. The absence of embryos does not negate a filarial diagnosis, especially in symptomatic cases like elephantiasis. *Bacillus lymphangiticus* (resembling *B. subtilis*) has been reported as a cause of filarial lymphangitis.
differential_diagnosis: **For Filaria bancrofti:** - **Elephantiasis**: Must be differentiated from Elephantiasis Graecorum (leprosy). - **Elephantoid Fever**: May be confused with malarial paroxysms. - **Varicose Groin Glands**: Should be differentiated from hernia, especially when the hernial sac contains omental contents. **For Loa loa:** - **Transient Swellings**: May be misdiagnosed as rheumatism, erythema nodosum, or angioneurotic oedema.
management_and_clinical_course: Management varies by the specific filarial infection and its clinical manifestations: **For Filaria bancrofti:** - **General**: Salvarsan, arsenophenylglycin, and similar remedies have shown no special effect on adult filarial worms. - **Elephantoid Fever**: Treatment involves rest in bed, elevation of the affected part, laxatives, and local applications. - **Lymph Scrotum**: Local applications and suspension of the scrotum. For severe hypertrophy, surgical excision of the blubbery tissues is performed, taking care to protect testicles and ensure sound tissue for closure flaps. Wounds typically heal readily, though lymph outpouring can delay healing. - **Varicose Groin Glands**: Surgical intervention is generally not advisable. - **Filarial Abscesses**: Treatment is similar to that for other abscesses. - **Chyluria**: Requires rest in bed, laxatives, and restriction of fluids and fats. Patients should refrain from active exercise and conditions causing fatigue. Drugs are of little value, and the condition has a tendency to spontaneously disappear and reappear. - **Elephantiasis**: Surgical treatment is common, with amputation indicated if an extremity becomes too burdensome. Lymphangioplasty (introduction of silk threads to create channels to normal lymphatics) has generally not achieved permanent success, with new channels quickly obliterating or becoming infected. Castellani recommended daily injections of Merck’s fibrolysin (2-4 cc for 3-6 months), followed by tight bandaging (flannel or rubber), possibly with massage, into the affected part or gluteal region. When the limb shrinks and skin smoothes, long strips of skin and subcutaneous tissue may be dissected out and adjacent edges sutured. - **Scrotal Elephantiasis Surgery (Fauntleroy's Method)**: Pre-operative preparation includes bed rest, thorough scrubbing, and antiseptics (alcohol or iodine). The lithotomy position is used. A horseshoe-shaped incision frees the penis, and subsequent lateral incisions reach the testicles. The testicles are stripped from surrounding blubbery tissue. Affected tunicae vaginales may contain fluid that needs drainage. In some cases (60%), one testicle may need removal due to extensive disease. Hernial complications and undescended testicles must be considered. The penis is freed, and sound skin from the horseshoe flap and pre-existing prepuce is used to construct coverings for the penis and testicles. Lateral flaps are sutured to form a new scrotum, leaving space for drainage. This procedure has a reported mortality of 5%, though Fauntleroy reported no deaths in 149 operations for tumors up to 85 pounds. **For Loa loa:** - **Ocular Worms**: If worms are noted in the eye region, a local anaesthetic can be used, and the worm seized with forceps and extracted through a small incision. Elliot recommended hot fomentations, then cocaine instillation upon appearance under the conjunctiva, followed by seizing the worm with forceps, passing a silk ligature through the conjunctival fold to secure it, tying the ligature, and extracting through an incision. - **Calabar Swellings**: Cooling local applications or ichthyol ointment may be applied. **For Onchocerca volvulus:** - The subcutaneous tumors are easily enucleated. **For Dracunculus medinensis:** - Douching the point of exit with water can cause the uterus to empty over approximately three weeks. After this, intermittent traction by winding the worm around an object (e.g., toothpick) can be used for gradual extraction. Excessive force may cause the worm to break, leading to abscess formation or sloughing. Macfie reported success with intravenous tartar emetic (1 grain every other day, total 6 grains), which rapidly reduced inflammation and discharge. **For Acanthocheilonema perstans and Filaria demarquayi/ozzardi:** No specific treatments are mentioned, consistent with their generally non-pathogenic nature.

tables.title: Characteristics of Filarial Worms
rows: Filaria bancrofti
Male 40 by 0.1 mm. Female 90 by 0.28 mm. Smooth cuticle. Bulbous anterior extremity. Occupy lymphatic glands and vessels.

Sheathed, 300 by 7.5 microns. Distance from head to V spot 90 microns; to break in cells 50 microns. Tail rather straight. Terminal cells do not fill up tail end. Nocturnal periodicity in peripheral circulation.
Transmitted by mosquitoes, Culex fatigans and Stegomyia pseudo-xxx scutellaris. Causes elephantiasis, lymph scrotum, chyluria, etc.
Loa loa
Male 27 by 0.3 mm. Female 55 by 0.4 mm. Cuticle tuberculated. Anterior extremity like truncated cone. Wanders in subcutaneous tissues.

Sheathed, 240 × 7 microns. Distance from head to V spot 65 microns; to break in cells 40 microns. Cork-screw tail which is completely filled up with terminal cells. Diurnal periodicity in peripheral circulation.
Transmitted by species of a biting fly—Chrysops. Causes calabar swellings. Worms often visit ocular region.
Acanthocheilonema perstans
Male 40 by 0.07 mm. Female 75 by 0.1 mm. Cuticle smooth. Tip of tail shows 2 triangular processes. Found about root of mesentery.
Without sheaths, 200 by 5 microns. Posterior two-thirds tapers to blunt ending. Distance from head to V spot 49 microns; to break in cells 34 microns. Persists in circulation both day and night.
Transmitting agent not surely known. Mosquitoes and ticks suggested. No pathogenicity.
Onchocerca volvulus
Male 30 by 0.14 mm. Female usually fragmented. Possibly 75 by 0.36 mm. Cuticle striated. Found coiled up in cyst-like tumors under skin.
Without sheaths, 250 by 7.5 microns. Found in cyst-like spaces of tumors. Not in peripheral circulation.
Method of transmission unknown. Causes small cystic tumors, under skin of thorax especially.
Dracunculus medinensis
Male from Leiper’s monkey 22 mm. Female 80 to 90 cm. long by 1.6 mm. wide. Smooth white body. Anchoring hook at tail end. Female lives in subcutaneous tissue of lower extremity.
Without sheaths. 600 × 20 microns. Long slender tail. Cuticle striated. Extruded from break in skin of patient.
Embryos swallowed by Cyclops. Man drinks water containing Cyclops.
